lead: Enterprise blockchains are shared ledgers run by a known group. They add permissioning, identity and integration to the ledger. Permissioning means only approved organisations join. Identity means each user signs with a certificate. Integration means the ledger talks to ERP, payment and AI systems. AI adds prediction and model audit on top of trusted data. Banks use this for trade finance, manufacturers for supplier records, and auditors for model checks.
prereq: You need: chaincode, scalability limits and IoT data patterns.

blocks.text: A consortium network is a blockchain owned by several firms, not one firm and not the public. Members know each other. A membership service issues a certificate to every user and node. A channel is a private subnet; only channel members see its transactions. This is permissioning: read and write rights are explicit. It suits trade finance, insurance claims and supplier records where privacy and legal identity matter (see finance).

Blockchain as a Service (BaaS) is cloud hosting for such networks. A provider runs peers, orderers, certificates and chaincode lifecycle. The enterprise pays a monthly fee and connects its ERP through APIs. ERP integration posts a hash of an invoice or purchase order to the ledger. The full document stays in the ERP database. BaaS lowers setup cost, but the provider becomes an operational dependency. Legal contracts still sit outside.

An oracle is a service that writes outside facts to the chain. It signs the data, so readers know which oracle supplied it. On-chain data is small and shared: hashes, amounts, status flags. Off-chain data is the raw document, image or sensor stream. Keep private data off-chain and store a pointer plus hash.

items: Enterprise hashes an input record and logs the input hash.
The AI service reads approved off-chain data.
The AI service stores a model hash on the chain.
The enterprise requests a prediction and receives a score plus hash.
An auditor checks the model hash and the input hash.

blocks.text: AI is used for fraud detection, demand forecasting and credit scoring. The ledger does not make a model truthful; it makes the model version and inputs auditable. This is model provenance. A chaincode can release payment only when the prediction cites an approved model hash. The raw training set never goes on-chain.

sections.h3: Model provenance, federated learning and audit

blocks.text: Model provenance is the record of which model, which data version and which settings produced a prediction. Store a model hash, a data-version hash and a prediction log. An auditor reruns the model hash and checks the log. Federated learning trains a shared model across firms without moving raw data. Each firm sends model updates; the ledger records update hashes and training rounds. This gives audit trails with data minimisation.

A model card can list training data, accuracy and owner; its hash goes on-chain. That gives reproducible checks. The pattern is: raw data off-chain, hashes on-chain, AI off-chain, audit on-chain. Governance decides who approves models and oracles. If an oracle lies, the hash is valid but the fact is false; trust the oracle process. Store hashes and pointers, never full models or private training data, on-chain.

spec.aria: A raw input and an AI model, both off-chain, are hashed to 32 bytes each and combined into a 64-byte log entry; below, a short bar for one day of 64 kB and a long bar for 30 days of 1.92 MB.

examples.question: An enterprise logs 1,000 AI predictions per day. Each log stores a 32-byte input hash and a 32-byte model hash. Find the storage per day in bytes and kB, and the storage for 30 days in kB and MB. Use 1 kB = 1000 B and 1 MB = 1000 kB.
steps: Each log stores H_in = 32 B and H_model = 32 B, so one log uses 32 B + 32 B = 64 B.
For N = 1,000 predictions/day: storage/day = N × (H_in + H_model) = 1,000 × 64 B = 64,000 B.
Convert to kB: 64,000 B ÷ 1,000 B/kB = 64 kB.
Convert to MB: 1,920 kB ÷ 1,000 kB/MB = 1.92 MB.
examples.answer: The 30-day hash log needs 1.92 MB; raw inputs and models stay off-chain.
examples.check:
n = 1000
h_in = 32
h_model = 32
per_day_b = n * (h_in + h_model)
per_day_kb = per_day_b / 1000
month_kb = per_day_kb * 30
month_mb = month_kb / 1000
print(per_day_b)
print(per_day_kb)
print(month_kb)
print(month_mb)

traps: Storing full training data or model weights on-chain; store a 32-byte hash and an off-chain pointer.
A hash proves integrity, not that the oracle's fact is true.
A consortium chain is not a public chain with a login screen; membership and endorsement are enforced.
BaaS is managed hosting; it does not remove governance or key management.
Use 1 kB = 1000 B as in the example; 1 KiB = 1024 B changes the answer.

quiz.a: A permissioned ledger shared by known firms, with no single owner.
It is large and private; store a hash and pointer.

quiz.q: 500 predictions/day, 32 B + 32 B hashes. 30-day MB at 1 MB = 1000 kB?
How does a model hash help an auditor?
quiz.a: Identifies the exact model; rerun it and compare the log.
Cloud hosting for nodes, identity and chaincode.

quiz.q: Why does federated learning fit enterprise chains?
quiz.a: Share model updates, not raw data; the ledger records hashes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry work here is mostly integration: ERP connectors, oracle services, model registries and audit dashboards. Research looks at verifiable AI, zero-knowledge proofs for model checks and privacy-preserving federated learning. Search next for blockchain as a service, model provenance and federated learning audit.
